questions.stem: The Ottoman Empire takes its name from which ruler, who founded the state in north-western Anatolia around 1300?
options: Orhan
Mehmed II
Suleiman I
Osman I
questions.explanation: The Ottomans were named after Osman I, whose small state in north-western Anatolia (modern Türkiye) grew at the expense of the Byzantine Empire. Orhan was Osman's son and successor, who carried on the expansion. Mehmed II and Suleiman I ruled much later, in the 1400s and 1500s.

questions.stem: Which city, captured from the Byzantines in 1326, became the first major Ottoman capital?
options: Edirne
Konya
Ankara
Bursa
questions.explanation: Osman's forces besieged Bursa for years, and his son Orhan took it in 1326 and made it the capital; nearby Nicaea (Iznik) fell soon after. Edirne, in Europe, became the capital later in the 1300s, before Constantinople. Konya had been the capital of the earlier Seljuk sultanate, not the Ottomans.

questions.stem: In 1453 Sultan Mehmed II captured which city, the capital of the Byzantine Empire?
options: Constantinople
Belgrade
Vienna
Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Mehmed II took Constantinople on 29 May 1453, ending more than a thousand years of Byzantine rule there, and it became the Ottoman capital, increasingly known as Istanbul. Belgrade was taken later, by Suleiman in 1521. The Ottomans besieged Vienna twice but never captured it.

questions.stem: Which weapon was especially important in Mehmed II's capture of Constantinople?
options: Longbowmen who out-ranged the Byzantine crossbowmen
Huge cannons that battered the city's land walls
Catapults that hurled Greek fire over the walls
War elephants that broke through the city gates
questions.explanation: Mehmed had giant bronze cannons cast, some by an engineer named Orban, and they pounded the famous land walls for weeks until they could be breached. Greek fire was a Byzantine weapon used mainly at sea, not an Ottoman one. Mehmed also had ships dragged overland into the Golden Horn to get around the chain that blocked the harbour.

questions.stem: What happened to the great church of Hagia Sophia soon after the Ottoman conquest in 1453?
options: It was closed and left to fall into ruin
It was converted into a mosque
It was demolished to build a palace
It was handed to the Pope as a cathedral
questions.explanation: Mehmed II had Hagia Sophia converted into a mosque, and minarets were later added around it. It was not destroyed; the building still stands in Istanbul. It became a museum only in 1934 under the Turkish Republic, and was made a mosque again in 2020.

questions.stem: Who were the janissaries?
options: The sultan's chief ministers who ran the government
Religious judges who applied Islamic law in the courts
Cavalrymen paid with land grants in the provinces
Elite infantry soldiers loyal to the sultan
questions.explanation: The janissaries were the sultan's elite foot soldiers, recruited largely through the devshirme and trained to be loyal to him alone. The chief ministers were the viziers, led by the grand vizier. Cavalrymen paid with grants of land were the sipahis, a separate part of the army.

questions.stem: What was the devshirme?
options: The right of each religious community to run its own courts and schools
A levy of Christian boys, converted to Islam and trained to serve the sultan
A tax paid in coin by Christian and Jewish subjects instead of serving
A grant of land given to cavalrymen in return for fighting in the sultan's army
questions.explanation: Under the devshirme, officials took boys mainly from Christian families in the Balkans, converted them and trained them as janissaries or palace officials. The tax paid by non-Muslims was the jizya, and land grants to cavalrymen were timars, so both describe other parts of the system. Some devshirme recruits rose to the very top, including the architect Sinan and several grand viziers.

questions.stem: Under what historians call the millet system, how were Christian and Jewish communities in the Ottoman Empire generally treated?
options: They had exactly the same legal status and paid the same taxes as Muslims
They were banned from all trade and confined inside separate walled towns of their own
They kept their faith and ran matters such as marriage under their own leaders
They were forced to convert to Islam or else leave the empire entirely
questions.explanation: Religious communities were allowed to practise their faith and manage much of their own family law, education and charity through their own religious leaders, such as the Greek Orthodox patriarch. They were not equal to Muslims, though: they paid the jizya tax and faced some restrictions. This toleration is why many Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 settled in Ottoman cities.

questions.stem: Non-Muslim subjects of the Ottoman sultans paid the jizya. What was it?
options: A share of every harvest that all farmers paid, whatever their religion
A fee charged to every pilgrim entering the holy cities of Mecca and Medina
A fine paid by Christian families who refused to hand over a son
A yearly tax on non-Muslim men, who could then practise their own religion
questions.explanation: The jizya was a tax on adult non-Muslim men (women, children and the very poor were usually exempt), and in return the state protected them and allowed them to keep their faith. Land and harvest taxes were separate and were paid by Muslims too. Families could not buy their way out of the devshirme with a fine; boys were simply selected.

questions.stem: Why did Selim I's conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate (1516–1517) greatly raise the Ottoman sultans' standing in the Muslim world?
options: It gave them Constantinople, the holiest city in Islam
It made them guardians of Mecca and Medina, strengthening their claim to the caliphate
It gave them Baghdad, where the Abbasid caliphs had built the House of Wisdom
It brought Safavid Persia under their rule and united all Muslims in a single empire
questions.explanation: By defeating the Mamluks, Selim I took Syria, Egypt and the Hejaz, so the Ottomans now protected Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem. As guardians of Islam's holiest cities, the sultans claimed leadership of the Muslim world as caliphs. Baghdad was taken later, by Suleiman in 1534, and Persia was ruled by the rival Safavid dynasty, which the Ottomans never conquered.

questions.stem: Ottomans called Suleiman the Magnificent by a title meaning:
options: the Thunderbolt
the Lawgiver
the Conqueror
the Grim
questions.explanation: Suleiman (ruled 1520–1566) was known as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, because his reign brought together and updated the empire's law codes. 'The Conqueror' (Fatih) was Mehmed II, who took Constantinople. 'The Grim' was Selim I and 'the Thunderbolt' was the earlier sultan Bayezid I.

questions.stem: At the Battle of Mohács in 1526, Suleiman's army destroyed the army of which kingdom, whose young king died fleeing the battle?
options: Poland
Venice
Russia
Hungary
questions.explanation: At Mohács, Suleiman crushed the Hungarian army and King Louis II drowned while retreating, and much of Hungary later came under Ottoman rule. This opened the way into central Europe after his capture of Belgrade (1521) and Rhodes (1522). Poland's king would later help lift the siege of Vienna in 1683.

questions.stem: What was the outcome of Suleiman's first siege of Vienna in 1529?
options: The city fell and became the capital of a new Ottoman province in Austria
The Habsburgs counter-attacked and recaptured Belgrade and the rest of Hungary
A treaty forced Vienna to pay the sultan yearly tribute while staying under Habsburg rule
Bad weather, supply problems and a stubborn defence forced the Ottomans to withdraw
questions.explanation: Heavy rain slowed Suleiman's march, so much of his heavy artillery was left behind, and with winter approaching and supplies short he lifted the siege in October. Vienna was never captured by the Ottomans. Vienna remained a Habsburg stronghold, and the Ottomans did not besiege it again until 1683.

questions.stem: Why do historians see the second siege of Vienna in 1683 as a turning point?
options: It ended the Ottoman Empire, which was then divided among its enemies
It forced the Ottomans to move their capital from Istanbul back to Bursa
Its failure marked the limit of Ottoman expansion, and the empire then began losing land in Europe
It was the first time an Ottoman army had ever reached and besieged a city in central Europe
questions.explanation: A relief army led by the Polish king Jan III Sobieski defeated the besiegers in 1683, and in the war that followed the Ottomans lost Hungary (Treaty of Karlowitz, 1699). An Ottoman army had already reached Vienna in 1529, so it was not the first time. The empire itself survived until after the First World War.

questions.stem: Who was Mimar Sinan?
options: The astronomer who built an observatory in Istanbul
The chief architect who designed the Süleymaniye and Selimiye mosques
The grand vizier who wrote Suleiman's new law codes
The admiral whose galley fleet dominated the Mediterranean in the 1530s
questions.explanation: Sinan, chief architect to three sultans, designed hundreds of buildings, including the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul and the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, which he considered his masterpiece. He began as a devshirme recruit and served as a military engineer before becoming an architect. The admiral who dominated the Mediterranean was Hayreddin Barbarossa.

questions.stem: Why are Ottoman mosques decorated mainly with geometric patterns, plant designs and calligraphy rather than pictures of people?
options: Ottoman law banned all painting of people anywhere in the empire
Coloured tiles were cheaper than paint, so builders used simple shapes
Ottoman artists had not yet learnt the skills to draw or paint the human figure
Islamic tradition avoids images of people and animals in places of worship
questions.explanation: Islamic religious tradition discourages images of living beings in mosques, so artists developed complex geometric patterns, flowing plant designs and Arabic calligraphy of verses from the Qur'an. Painting of people was not banned everywhere: Ottoman court artists painted detailed miniatures of sultans, battles and festivals for books. The patterns rely on advanced geometry, not a lack of skill.

questions.stem: What role did coffee houses play in Ottoman cities such as Istanbul from the 1500s?
options: Places of worship where Muslims gathered for Friday prayers
Government offices where taxes were paid and recorded
Barracks where the janissaries ate and slept between long military campaigns
Meeting places where men talked, played games and heard the latest news
questions.explanation: Coffee houses spread through Ottoman cities in the 1500s as places where men met to drink coffee, talk, play games such as backgammon and listen to storytellers. Because people discussed news and politics there, some sultans tried to close them, but they kept coming back. Friday prayers were held in mosques, not coffee houses.

questions.stem: Besides the prayer hall, what did the Süleymaniye Mosque complex built for Suleiman in Istanbul include?
options: Barracks for the janissaries and a weapons store
The sultan's palace and the treasury of the empire
A slave market, a coin mint and a large customs house
Religious schools, a hospital and a public kitchen
questions.explanation: Large Ottoman mosques were built as complexes (külliye) that served the city, and the Süleymaniye included madrasas (religious schools), a hospital, a public kitchen that fed the poor, baths and tombs. The sultan's palace was Topkapi, a separate site. These complexes show how the empire combined religion, education and care for the sick.

questions.stem: Ottoman writers presented the conquest of Constantinople as God's will and the fulfilment of a prophecy, while the Byzantine historian Doukas described it as a catastrophe for Christians. What should a historian conclude?
options: The Ottoman account must be right because the winners kept the fullest official records
The Byzantine account must be right because it was written by Christians who lived nearby
Neither account can be used, because a source showing bias has no historical value
Each account reflects its writer's faith and side, so both must be checked against other evidence
questions.explanation: Both kinds of source were shaped by the writers' religion and loyalties, so a historian compares them with each other and with other evidence such as archaeology and letters. Winning a war does not make an account accurate, and being close to events does not remove bias. Biased sources are still very useful, especially for showing how different groups understood the same event.

questions.stem: Some Christian families in the Balkans dreaded the devshirme, while others hoped a son would be chosen. What best explains both reactions?
options: The boys stayed Christian and lived at home, so families lost very little
Losing a son to a new faith was painful, but recruits could rise to wealth and high office
Only sons of rich families were taken, so poorer families were jealous of them
Recruits returned home after five years of service with farmland and a pension from the sultan
questions.explanation: Families lost their sons, who were converted to Islam and rarely came home, which caused real grief. Yet devshirme boys were educated in the palace system and some became governors, generals or even grand viziers, which could also benefit their families. Recruiters mostly took boys from rural families, and the boys did not return home after a set term.
